Letter: SNAP is needed most when the economy sours 
 Letter: SNAP is needed most when the economy sours
 A message from the National Women's Law Center concerning the announcement by the Trump administration of restoring only half funding the SNAP benefits is projected on the U.S. Department of Agriculture building, Monday, Nov. 3, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/John McDonnell)
 By  Debbie Baskin | The Public Forum  | Nov. 21, 2026, 6:00 a.m. | Updated: 7:14 a.m. Comment
 Add as Preferred Source
 The panhandlers are at the ward house, the grocery store, near the dance studios and climbing gyms where my kids are. I want to help but it is overwhelming to see so many in need.
 Food banks across Utah are facing major strain — rising costs and more Utahns needing help. During hard economic times, both donations and grants dramatically decline.
 There is a better way: the SNAP program (food stamps) allows families, people with disabilities, seniors and veterans to buy the food they need: meat, fruit and vegetables. Food that not only satiates but helps bodies stay healthy. 
 Since July, 2025, when H.R.1 was enacted, 5.5 million people have been cut off from the SNAP program, including 2 million children.
 Yes, we need to balance the federal budget, but to paraphrase Neil Rickard, society will pay for this. We can pay upfront through taxes to provide emergency food assistance, or we will pay later through increased medical costs, homeless services, and children with poor educational outcomes. 
 Prevention is not only compassionate, it is financially wise. Please call your members of Congress and ask them to protect SNAP benefits!
 Debbie Baskin, Salt Lake City
